Array_Indexing_Needs_Parentheses.short_definition: Learners believe that accessing an array element in Processing requires extra parentheses around the index expression, e.g. numbers[(i)] instead of numbers[i].
Array_Indexing_Needs_Parentheses.why_incorrect: While numbers[(0)] is syntactically valid, the parentheses inside the square brackets are unnecessary. The parentheses add no functional value unless the index expression involves multiple operations and needs to be grouped for precedence, e.g. numbers[(i + 1) * 2].
indicators: Array access uses parentheses directly inside brackets: something[(index)]
The parentheses contain only a literal or a simple variable
There is no operator precedence reason for the parentheses
when_not_a_misconception: Parentheses are used because the index expression involves arithmetic, e.g. values[(i + 1) * 2]

examples_misconception_present.code: println(values[(2)]);
examples_misconception_present.explanation: Unnecessary parentheses around a simple literal index

examples_misconception_present.code: println(values[(i)]);
examples_misconception_present.explanation: Unnecessary parentheses around a variable index

examples_not_present.explanation: Parentheses are necessary due to operator precedence

Array_Init_Needs_Curly_Brackets.short_definition: Learners believe that curly brackets {} are necessary to create an array of a specific length, rather than to initialize it with specific values.
Array_Init_Needs_Curly_Brackets.why_incorrect: In Processing, curly brackets {} are used to define the contents of an array, not its length. The curly bracket syntax is used when you want to create and fill an array in a single step. For instance, int[] array = { 5, -105, 20 }; creates an array containing the values 5, -105, and 20: f you want to create an array with a specific length (but no initial values), you need to use the new keyword along with square brackets [].
indicators: Using curly brackets with a single number, indicating the learner thinks this sets the array length
Looping over an array initialized with curly brackets containing a single number
Assigning numeric values inside curly brackets to a non-numeric array type (e.g., boolean[], String[]).
when_not_a_misconception: Using curly brackets {} to initialize an array with multiple specific values.

examples_misconception_present.code: boolean[] array = { 3 };
examples_misconception_present.explanation: Learner believes that curly brackets set the length of the boolean array to 3

examples_misconception_present.code:
int[] array = { 5 };
array[2] = 1;
examples_misconception_present.explanation: Learner believes that curly brackets set the length of the array to 5, leading to an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when trying to access index 2

examples_not_present.explanation: Correctly using curly brackets to initialize an array with specific values

Array_Length_as_Number.short_definition: Learners believe that the length of an array should be accessed using a fixed number, rather than using the .length property. This leads to code that only works correctly as long as the array has exactly the hardcoded length, and breaks otherwise.
Array_Length_as_Number.why_incorrect: Hardcoding array lengths makes the code fragile and less flexible. If the array changes in size (e.g. because of different initialization or because it’s replaced), the loop may no longer behave correctly and may throw runtime errors such as ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. The correct way to access all elements of an array is the use of the built-in .length property, which always reflects the actual size of the array.
indicators: Array length is accessed using a fixed number in loops or conditions
No use of the .length property on the array
Use of fixed number which obviously seems to be related to other known array sizes or variables in the code, e.g., when initializing multiple arrays of the same size
when_not_a_misconception: The fixed number is used for a specific purpose unrelated to an array's length, e.g. accessing a specific index
A variable representing the length is used

examples_misconception_present.explanation: Using a fixed number (10) instead of data.length in the head of the loop
Using a fixed number (10) instead of foo.length or foo2.length in the loop body
Using a fixed number (10) instead of foo.length when initializing foo2 when both arrays are related as implied by their identical sizes and use in the loop

examples_not_present.explanation: Correctly using foo.length to fill foo2 based on the actual length of foo and using n for the loop condition

Array_Length_Only_in_Loop_Condition.short_definition: Learners believe that the .length property of an array can only be used inside loop conditions (typically in for loops). They might not realize that .length is a general property of arrays and can be used in any part of the code.
Array_Length_Only_in_Loop_Condition.why_incorrect: .length is a public property of every array in Processing and can be used anywhere in the code where the array’s length is needed, not just in loops.
indicators: Avoiding .length outside of a loop conditions and hardcoding its value
when_not_a_misconception: .length appears outside of loop conditions, eg. in loop bodies or outside loops

examples_misconception_present.explanation: Fixed number (5) is used both when initializing array2 and when wanting to fill array2 with decreasing values, while .length is correctly used in the loop condition

examples_misconception_present.code:
int[] arrayToCopy = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
int[] copy = new int[5];
examples_misconception_present.explanation: Fixed number (5) is used instead of arrayToCopy.length when initializing the copy array

examples_not_present.explanation: .length is used in the loop body, outside the loop condition

examples_not_present.code:
int[] arrayToCopy = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
int[] copy = new int[arrayToCopy.length];
examples_not_present.explanation: .length is correctly used to determine the size of the copy array
No concrete evidence of the misconception since n is representing the length of the arrays

Arrays_Always_Contain_Data.short_definition: Learners believe that arrays are always automatically populated with meaningful or usable values immediately after declaration, such as fully initialized objects for reference types.
Arrays_Always_Contain_Data.why_incorrect: In Processing, arrays are not initialized with values that learners might consider “meaningful” data. Primitive types are given standard defaults – for example, integers become 0, floats become 0.0, and booleans become false. But reference types, such as custom objects, are initialized with null, meaning that no actual object has been created or assigned yet.
indicators: Trying to access a null reference as if it were an object resulting in a NullPointerException
Using objects in arrays without initializing them first
when_not_a_misconception: Properly initializing objects in an array before use
Using primitive types in arrays which are automatically initialized with default values

examples_misconception_present.code:
Ball[] balls = new Ball[2];
println(balls[0].x);
examples_misconception_present.explanation: Accessing a property (x) of a null reference (balls[0]) in the balls array
Calling a method (draw()) on null references in the balls array

examples_not_present.explanation: Properly initializing objects in the balls array before accessing their properties
Using primitive types in the numbers array which are automatically initialized with default values

Arrays_Empty_At_Beginning.short_definition: Learners believe that arrays are completely empty after being created. They assume that the arrays contain “nothing at all” and must be manually filled with data.
Arrays_Empty_At_Beginning.why_incorrect: In Processing, arrays are not “empty” after initialization. Upon initialization, every element in the array automatically holds either a default value or a null reference, depending on the type of the array. Array elements of primitive types can be used immediately.
indicators: Assuming that primitive type arrays need to be explicitly filled with values before use
when_not_a_misconception: Creating a new array with the desired size and copying the old elements into it
Over-allocating an array and tracking the current count separately
Using ArrayList or other dynamic data structures instead of arrays

examples_misconception_present.explanation: Unnecessary initialization, since int arrays are automatically initialized to 0
Unnecessary initialization, since boolean arrays are automatically initialized to false

examples_not_present.explanation: Correctly using the automatically initialized values of the int array
Correctly initializing objects in the PVector array

Arrays_Grow.short_definition: Learners believe that the length of an array is flexible, so they can freely add or remove elements.
Arrays_Grow.why_incorrect: In Processing arrays have a fixed length that is determined when the array is created and cannot be changed afterwards. To store more elements you must create a new array with the desired size and copy the old elements into it.
indicators: Code attempts to write beyond the last valid index of the array
Creating an array of length 0 and then trying to add elements
Trying to use methods or operators that do not exist for arrays in Processing, e.g., trying to use add(), append(), or similar methods that do not exist for arrays in Processing.
when_not_a_misconception: Creating a new array with the desired size and copying the old elements into it
Over-allocating an array and tracking the current count separately
Using ArrayList or other dynamic data structures instead of arrays

examples_misconception_present.explanation: Attempting to add elements to an array (c) of length 0
Writing beyond the last valid index

examples_not_present.explanation: Correctly creating an array (xPosTemp) with increased size and copying elements
Over-allocating an array and tracking the current count separately

Inner_Arrays_Uniform.short_definition: Learners believe that in a multidimensional array (e.g., a 2D array), all inner arrays must have the same size. They assume a rectangular or grid-likestructure is mandatory. Therefore, they may be confused when seeing or working with jagged arrays (arrays of arrays with different lengths).
Inner_Arrays_Uniform.why_incorrect: In Processing, a multidimensional array is an array of arrays, and the inner arrays do not need to be the same length. Only when you use a uniform initialization (e.g. new int[3][4]) are all inner arrays created with the same size automatically. However, you can freely construct a multidimensional array with varying inner sizes (commonly referred to as a jagged array).
indicators: Using nested loops that assume all inner arrays have the same length
Believing that a 2D array must always be initialized with two dimensions at once
Leaving last elements of inner arrays uninitialized to maintain uniform length
when_not_a_misconception: Using nested loops that correctly handle varying inner array lengths
Creating jagged arrays intentionally for specific use cases

examples_misconception_present.explanation: Assuming all inner arrays have the same length by using jagged[0].length in the inner loop
Using null to fill an inner array to maintain uniform length

examples_not_present.explanation: Creating a jagged array with inner arrays of different lengths
Correctly handling varying inner array lengths in nested loops

Loops_for_Array_Index_Access.short_definition: Learners tend to believe that a loop is always needed to access an element of an array, even if the index of the respective element is already known.
Loops_for_Array_Index_Access.why_incorrect: Accessing an element of an array does not require a loop when the index of the element is already known. Using a loop in such cases adds unnecessary complexity and inefficiency to the code. Instead, the element can be accessed directly using its index.
indicators: Using a loop to access an element of an array with a known index
if statements inside loops that check for a specific index to access an element
when_not_a_misconception: Using loops to access elements of an array when the indices are not known in advance.

examples_misconception_present.explanation: Using a loop to access the element at known index declared in variable z (3)
Using a loop to access the element at fixed known index (3)

examples_not_present.explanation: Directly accessing the element at known index (3) without a loop

One_Loop_per_Array.short_definition: Learners think that each array must be iterated in its own separate loop, even when arrays are structurally aligned (i.e., same length) and logically connected. This leads to code duplication and hides the fact that the data in the arrays is conceptually linked at corresponding indices.
One_Loop_per_Array.why_incorrect: While separate loops are not syntactically wrong, they introduce unnecessary redundancy and obscure the structural relationship between arrays. They also make the code longer and harder to maintain, increase the likelihood of mistakes (e.g. mismatched loop lengths or inconsistent logic) and they reduce clarity by hiding that the index represents the same conceptual entity (e.g. ball, player etc.) across multiple arrays. Using one loop for parallel arrays reveals this connection and improves code quality.
indicators: Multiple independent loops to iterate over related arrays, even when these arrays are of the same length and should be processed together
when_not_a_misconception: Using separate loops for arrays of different lengths
Processing logic between loops is fundamentally different

examples_misconception_present.explanation: Using separate loops to initialize related arrays position and speed
Using separate loops to initialize and draw the same array vec

examples_not_present.explanation: Using a single loop to initialize related arrays position and speed
